newsitem.title: DENMARK: FORECAST-Denmark sees lower 96, 97 budget deficits.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Denmark sees lower 96, 97 budget deficits.

text.p: Denmark's Finance Ministry cut on Tuesday its estimates for the 1996 and 1997 state budget deficits to 25.0 billion crowns and 5.9 billion crowns respectively.
The ministry's last estimates, announced in October, forecast a state budget deficit of 28.5 billion crowns for this year and 19.3 billion crowns for next year.
Earlier in December, the ministry provisionally cut its estimates for the 1997 state budget deficit by approximately seven billion crowns, to around 12 billion crowns.

Denmark's 1995 state budget shortfall was 31.2 billion crowns. The ministry's forecast also pointed to a public sector surplus of about two billion crowns in 1997, the first surplus since 1988, with a bigger plus expected for 1998.

"The public sector surplus is the result of tight fiscal policies over a period of many years combined with progress for the Danish economy," the ministry said in a statement accompanying its new estimates.
"The continuing improvement in the Danish economy means a reduction in state outgoings on unemployment benefits, as well as boosting the state's income from taxes and duties," it said.
"The Danish economy is at its strongest level in over 35 years, with all key indicators pointing in the right direction," Finance Minister Mogens Lykketoft said in the statement.
"Interest rates and inflation are low, the foreign debt is decreasing, unemployment is on the wane and the public sector budget is showing a surplus," he said.

The ministry's new forecast follows an encouraging Economy Ministry forecast earlier in December which gave Denmark's economy a clean bill of health but called for wage restraint in next spring's collective wage bargaining. --Chris Follett, Copenhagen newsroom +45-33969652
